# Case Study: Palmer Penguins {#sec-penguins}

Penguins is clean, and clean data invite you to skip the steps the
earlier chapters argue for. Fit the obvious model and it reports a
respectable $R^2$, four diagnostic plots with nothing alarming in
them, and coefficients that read sensibly; its residuals
nevertheless separate by sex, a variable the model never saw,
and none of the four standard plots shows it. This chapter runs the
whole arc of an analysis on that easy dataset, from scaffold to
deposited DOI, labels every step with the chapter that taught it,
and performs each step deliberately, including the ones that look
unnecessary. The arc is what you are practicing, so that it is
automatic when the data are difficult and the stakes are real; it
is also the worked model for the capstone project in
@sec-synthesis.

## The arc, step by step {#sec-penguins-arc}

The Palmer Penguins dataset [@horst2022palmerpenguins] is the
successor to `iris`. It has enough structure to exercise the full
arc of an analysis, from wrangling through description and
inference to reporting, and it does so without the eugenics
association that accompanies Fisher's irises, which he analyzed in
the *Annals of Eugenics*. The dataset is small enough that the
analysis runs in seconds.

@tbl-penguins-arc is the arc. Each row is a step of this chapter,
the chapter that taught it, and the check that tells you the step
is done. The capstone project in @sec-synthesis asks you to fill in
the same table for the HF-HOME study.

| Step | What you do here | Taught in | Done when |
|---|---|---|---|
| Scaffold | Create the compendium: layout, lockfile, container | @sec-rrtools, @sec-renv, @sec-docker, @sec-zzcollab | The pillar audit of @sec-zzcollab-audit passes |
| Clean | Map the missingness; drop only rows the model needs | @sec-wrangling, @sec-missing | The analytic `n` is computed and explained |
| Describe | Table 1 by the design variable | @sec-wrangling, @sec-missing | Missing values appear as a row, not silently |
| Visualize | Scatter plot by species, faceted by island | @sec-graphics | The plot motivates the model |
| Fit | Linear model of mass on flipper length and species | @sec-analysis-plan | The model was chosen before the coefficients were seen |
| Diagnose | Standard plots, then residuals against omitted variables | @sec-graphics | Every pattern is explained or reported |
| Report | Methods and results with computed numbers | @sec-quarto | No number in the prose is typed |
| Test | Assertions on the data and the model's statistics | @sec-testing | The suite fails when a planted bug is introduced |
| CI (continuous integration) | Tests and render on every push | @sec-ci, @sec-testing-ci | A failing test turns the job red |
| Deposit | Tag, archive, DOI (digital object identifier), README | @sec-git-solo-tags, @sec-federal | The DOI resolves and the README rebuilds the paper |

: The analysis arc, with the chapter that taught each step. Use it
as the checklist for the capstone. {#tbl-penguins-arc}

`palmerpenguins::penguins` holds 344 observations of three penguin
species collected on three islands of the Palmer Archipelago,
Antarctica, from 2007 to 2009.

| Variable | Type | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `species` | factor, 3 levels | Adelie, Chinstrap, Gentoo; the design variable |
| `island` | factor, 3 levels | Biscoe, Dream, Torgersen; largely aliased with species |
| `bill_length_mm`, `bill_depth_mm` | numeric | Bill morphology |
| `flipper_length_mm` | numeric | The predictor |
| `body_mass_g` | numeric | The outcome |
| `sex` | factor, 2 levels | Female, male; the variable with most missing values |
| `year` | integer | 2007, 2008, or 2009 |

: Variables in `palmerpenguins::penguins`. {#tbl-penguins-vars}

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** Penguins needs no imputation, has no join, and fits
in memory a thousand times over. Why does the chapter scaffold a
container, write tests, and set up CI for it?

**Answer.** Because the arc is the thing being practiced, and a
step skipped on easy data is a step not yet automatic on hard
data. The steps also catch real problems here: the cleaning step
decides the denominator, and the diagnostic step finds structure
the model omits. The cost of each step is minutes; the cost of
learning to skip them is paid on the first project where they
matter.
:::

## Scaffold and clean {#sec-penguins-clean}

### Scaffolding the compendium

Assemble the compendium by hand as @sec-zzcollab-assemble does, or
automate it. One way to automate it is the in-house `zzcollab`
framework (@sec-zzcollab-optional), shown here (display-only,
because it creates a project and builds an image):

```bash
mkdir penguins-analysis
cd penguins-analysis
zzc tidyverse            # scaffold the Five Pillars
make docker-build        # build the image
make r                   # enter R inside the container
```

`zzc tidyverse` writes the Five Pillars (@sec-zzcollab):
Dockerfile, `renv.lock`, `.Rprofile`, source-code directories, and
a README pointing at the data.[^zzc-profile] `make docker-build`
builds the image (slow on the first run; cached afterward), and
`make r` drops you into an R session inside it. Whichever route you
took, run the tool-neutral audit of @sec-zzcollab-audit before
writing analysis code; in a `zzcollab` project,
`make check-renv-no-fix` adds a report on whether the code,
`DESCRIPTION`, and `renv.lock` agree.

[^zzc-profile]: The `tidyverse` profile was formerly called
    `analysis`, and `zzc analysis` still works as a deprecated
    alias (as of the repository in October 2026).

### Mapping the missingness

```{r}
#| label: fig-penguins-missing
#| fig-cap: "Missingness map for the raw penguin data. Missingness is
#|   concentrated in `sex`, with two rows missing all four morphology
#|   measurements."
#| fig-alt: "Missingness map of the raw penguin data, one row per
#|   observation and one column per variable, with missing cells
#|   marked. The sex column shows scattered missing cells throughout;
#|   two rows are missing across all four morphology columns at
#|   once, appearing as short horizontal gaps."
#| fig-scap: "Missingness map for the raw penguin data"
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4
#| message: false
library(palmerpenguins)
library(naniar)

vis_miss(penguins)
```

```{r}
#| label: penguins-miss-summary
miss_var_summary(penguins)
```

Missingness is mostly in `sex`
(`r sum(is.na(penguins$sex))` rows,
`r round(100 * mean(is.na(penguins$sex)), 1)`%); two rows are
missing all four morphology measurements, plausibly a lost data
sheet for each bird.

::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'}
Ask a model to lay out the options for the missing `sex` values,
not to choose one.

> **Context.** I am analyzing `palmerpenguins::penguins` (344 rows;
> columns and types from `str(penguins)` pasted below). `sex` is
> missing in 11 rows; two rows are missing every morphology
> measurement. My planned model is
> `lm(body_mass_g ~ flipper_length_mm + species)`.
>
> **Constraints.** Do not recommend imputing `sex` from
> sex-specific distributions of other variables. Do not use the
> fraction missing as the criterion.
>
> **Criteria.** First say whether the planned model needs the rows
> with missing `sex` handled at all. Then, for a second model that
> adds `sex`, compare complete-case analysis with multiple
> imputation, stating for each the condition under which the
> coefficient estimates are unbiased.

*Failure mode.* Models often answer a different question: they
recommend handling `sex` although the planned model never uses it,
or they propose imputing sex 'from sex-specific distributions',
which presupposes the sex it is trying to fill in. A second common
error states that complete case is biased whenever data are
missing at random. *Check.* The answer should drop no row for the
planned model, and its condition for complete case should match
@sec-missing-complete-case. Fit the model with `sex` both ways
(`mice::mice()` with the outcome in the imputation model) and
compare the coefficients. A data dictionary is structure, not
data, so it may go to any approved tool (@sec-ai-governance).
:::

### Dropping only what the model needs

Complete-case analysis is defensible here, and the reason is not
that the missing fraction is small. Complete-case estimates of a
regression coefficient are unbiased when missingness does not
depend on the outcome once the model's covariates are held fixed
(@sec-missing-complete-case). Here the missingness plausibly
reflects field data collection rather than body mass, and the model
below does not use `sex` at all. Drop only the rows the analysis
needs, not every row with any gap, and record the choice:

```{r}
#| label: penguins-clean
penguins_clean <- tidyr::drop_na(penguins, body_mass_g,
                                 flipper_length_mm)
nrow(penguins_clean)
```

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
Assert the denominator you intend, and that no modeled column
carries a missing value.

```{r}
#| label: penguins-clean-verify
stopifnot(
  nrow(penguins) - nrow(penguins_clean) == 2,
  !anyNA(penguins_clean[c("body_mass_g", "flipper_length_mm",
                          "species")])
)
```
:::

The two rows missing every morphology measurement are dropped;
analyses use $n = `r nrow(penguins_clean)`$. The
`r sum(is.na(penguins_clean$sex))` further rows missing only `sex`
stay in, and Table 1 reports their `sex` as missing.

::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'}
**`na.omit()` drops rows the model does not need, and the model
still fits.** `na.omit(penguins)` and `tidyr::drop_na(penguins)`
with no columns named remove every row with any missing value:
`r nrow(na.omit(penguins))` rows remain instead of
`r nrow(penguins_clean)`. Nothing errors, the coefficients shift
only slightly on this dataset, and the methods section's
denominator is now wrong. On a dataset where the incidental column
is missing for a reason, the estimate moves too. Name the modeled
columns in `drop_na()`.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** A colleague argues that because only
`r round(100 * mean(!complete.cases(penguins)), 1)`% of rows have a
missing value, complete-case analysis is safe. What is wrong with
the argument, and what would make complete case unsafe here?

**Answer.** The fraction missing governs precision, not bias.
Complete-case coefficient estimates are unbiased when missingness
does not depend on the outcome given the covariates, whatever the
fraction. They would be biased if, say, the heaviest birds were
the ones whose mass went unrecorded because they could not be
weighed, since missingness would then depend on body mass itself.
:::

## Describe and visualize {#sec-penguins-describe}

### Table 1

`gtsummary` [@sjoberg2021gtsummary] produces a Table 1 from one
call. Stratify by the design variable, and keep missing values as a
visible row:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-penguins-table1
#| tbl-cap: "Characteristics of the analytic sample by species,
#|   median (first quartile, third quartile) or n (%)."
#| message: false
library(gtsummary)

penguins_clean |>
  tbl_summary(
    by = species,
    include = c(bill_length_mm, flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g,
                sex, island),
    missing_text = "Missing"
  ) |>
  add_overall() |>
  as_kable()
```

The table carries no row p-values: Table 1 describes the sample,
and inference belongs to the model fitted below. The island rows
show the design. Adelies appear on all three islands, Chinstraps
only on Dream, and Gentoos only on Biscoe, so species and island
are largely aliased: an island difference can be estimated only
among Adelies, and a model with both terms cannot separate them for
the other two species. Leaving island out of the model is a
modeling choice, not a finding that island does not matter.

One way to automate a journal-styled Table 1 is the in-house
`zztable1` package (@sec-lab-software), which takes a formula
(display-only):

```r
zztable1::table1(
  bill_length_mm + flipper_length_mm + body_mass_g + sex ~ species,
  data = penguins_clean, totals = TRUE, pvalue = FALSE,
  numeric_summary = "median_iqr", theme = "nejm"
)
```

Its `pvalue` argument defaults to `TRUE`, so a descriptive Table 1
needs `pvalue = FALSE` stated.

### Exploratory scatter plot

```{r}
#| label: fig-penguins-scatter
#| fig-cap: "Body mass against flipper length, colored by species and
#|   faceted by island. Three clear clusters emerge, and the
#|   within-cluster association motivates the model that follows."
#| fig-alt: "Scatter plot of body mass against flipper length,
#|   points colored by species and split into one panel per island.
#|   Three separated clusters are visible, with Gentoo heaviest and
#|   longest-flippered; within every cluster body mass rises with
#|   flipper length."
#| fig-scap: "Body mass against flipper length, by species"
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 4
library(ggplot2)

theme_set(theme_minimal())

ggplot(penguins_clean,
       aes(flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g, color = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
  labs(x = "Flipper length (mm)",
       y = "Body mass (g)",
       color = "Species") +
  facet_wrap(~ island)
```

The plot shows three clusters by species, with flipper length and
body mass strongly associated within each. Gentoos (Biscoe only)
are the heaviest and longest-flippered; Adelies (all three islands)
and Chinstraps (Dream only) overlap on mass and are distinguished
by bill length instead. The structure suggests the model: species
as a categorical predictor and flipper length as a continuous one.

### Exercises

1. Write a second Table 1 stratifying by year (2007, 2008, 2009)
   rather than species. What does the difference between the two
   tables tell you about the data collection design?

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
```{r}
#| label: soln-23-2
#| message: false
penguins_clean |>
  dplyr::group_by(year) |>
  dplyr::summarize(
    n            = dplyr::n(),
    across(c(bill_length_mm, flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g),
           \(x) round(mean(x), 1)),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

table(penguins_clean$year, penguins_clean$species)
```

```{r}
#| label: soln-23-2-spans
#| echo: false
span_of <- function(var, by) {
  means <- tapply(penguins_clean[[var]], penguins_clean[[by]], mean)
  diff(range(means))
}
mass_span_year     <- round(span_of("body_mass_g", "year"), -1)
mass_span_species  <- round(span_of("body_mass_g", "species"), -1)
flip_span_year     <- round(span_of("flipper_length_mm", "year"))
flip_span_species  <- round(span_of("flipper_length_mm", "species"))
```

The year-stratified table is unremarkable next to the species one.
Mean body mass spans about `r mass_span_year` g across years;
across species it spans about
`r format(mass_span_species, big.mark = ",")` g, and mean flipper
length moves `r flip_span_year` mm by year against
`r flip_span_species` mm by species. The between-year differences
are real but an order of magnitude smaller, and a Table 1
stratified by year would put them in front of the reader as though
they were the structure of the data.

The cross-tabulation says why they are small. Each species was
sampled in every year in roughly stable proportions, so year is
close to a nuisance variable and species is the design. A Table 1
that stratifies by the wrong variable looks reassuringly balanced
and tells you nothing, which is the point of the exercise.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** A reviewer asks you to add island to the model 'to
adjust for location'. What does @tbl-penguins-table1 tell you
about that request?

**Answer.** That most of the adjustment cannot be estimated. All
Chinstraps are on Dream and all Gentoos on Biscoe, so for those
species an island term and a species term are the same contrast,
and only the Adelie data can separate them. Reply with the
cross-tabulation, and offer an Adelie-only analysis of island if
the question matters.
:::

## Fit and diagnose {#sec-penguins-model}

### The fitted model

```{r}
#| label: penguins-fit
fit <- lm(body_mass_g ~ flipper_length_mm + species,
          data = penguins_clean)
broom::tidy(fit, conf.int = TRUE)
```

```{r}
#| label: penguins-glance
broom::glance(fit) |>
  dplyr::select(r.squared, adj.r.squared, sigma, df, nobs)
```

```{r}
#| label: penguins-species-gap
#| echo: false
mass_by_species <- tapply(
  penguins_clean$body_mass_g, penguins_clean$species, mean
)
gentoo_gap <- round(
  mass_by_species[["Gentoo"]] - mass_by_species[["Adelie"]], -1
)
gentoo_coef <- round(coef(fit)[["speciesGentoo"]], -1)
flipper_slope <- round(coef(fit)[["flipper_length_mm"]], 1)
```

Every number in the paragraphs that follow is computed by the
chunks above rather than typed in, which is the discipline of
@sec-quarto applied to the book's own case study.

The intercept is the predicted body mass of an Adelie penguin at a
flipper length of zero. It is an extrapolation far outside the data
and is not interpretable as anything; it exists to anchor the line.
The `flipper_length_mm` coefficient, `r flipper_slope` g per mm, is
the within-species slope: the expected difference in body mass
between two penguins of the same species whose flipper lengths
differ by one millimeter.

The species coefficients are where a reader most often misreads
the table. They are differences from Adelie *at the same flipper
length*, which is not the difference in average mass between the
species. Gentoos average about
`r format(gentoo_gap, big.mark = ",")` g heavier than Adelies; the
`speciesGentoo` coefficient is `r gentoo_coef` g, a small fraction
of that, because Gentoos also have much longer flippers and the
model has already credited the flipper-length term with most of
the difference. The adjusted coefficient answers 'how much heavier
is a Gentoo than an Adelie with the same flippers', a narrower
question than the one a reader assumes it answers.

```{r}
#| label: penguins-marginal
penguins_clean |>
  dplyr::group_by(species) |>
  dplyr::summarize(mean_mass = mean(body_mass_g),
                   mean_flipper = mean(flipper_length_mm),
                   .groups = "drop")
```

The $R^2$ of `r round(summary(fit)$r.squared, 2)` is respectable,
and on a clean morphometric dataset a respectable $R^2$ is not
evidence that the model is well specified. It says the predictors
and the outcome are related, and nothing about whether the
functional form is right or a variable is missing. That is what
the diagnostics are for.

### Diagnostic plots

```{r}
#| label: penguins-diag-stats
#| echo: false
cooks_max <- max(cooks.distance(fit))
n_big_resid <- sum(abs(rstandard(fit)) > 3)
fit_quad <- lm(body_mass_g ~ poly(flipper_length_mm, 2) + species,
               data = penguins_clean)
quad_p <- anova(fit, fit_quad)[2, "Pr(>F)"]
resid_sd <- round(tapply(residuals(fit), penguins_clean$species, sd))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-penguins-diagnostics
#| fig-cap: "The four standard `lm` diagnostic plots for the fitted
#|   model. Residuals versus fitted and scale-location test the
#|   mean and variance structure; the Q-Q plot tests the residual
#|   distribution; residuals versus leverage identifies influential
#|   observations."
#| fig-alt: "Four-panel regression diagnostic grid. Residuals against
#|   fitted values fall in two clusters, Adelie and Chinstrap on the
#|   left and Gentoo on the right, with a smoother that dips slightly
#|   in the middle. The normal quantile-quantile plot follows its
#|   reference line, with three points slightly above it in the upper
#|   tail. The scale-location smoother is nearly flat, a little lower
#|   at the largest fitted values. Residuals against leverage show
#|   every point far inside the Cook's distance contours."
#| fig-scap: "Diagnostic plots for the fitted penguin model"
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 6
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(fit)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

Read the four panels in turn, and say what each shows rather than
what it should show.

| Panel | What it shows for this fit | Conclusion |
|---|---|---|
| Residuals vs fitted | Two clusters (Adelie and Chinstrap left, Gentoo right) and a smoother with a shallow dip; a quadratic flipper term improves the fit (*p* = `r format(signif(quad_p, 2), scientific = FALSE)`) | Mild curvature; small next to the residual spread, worth a sensitivity analysis |
| Q-Q | Points on the reference line; three birds sit slightly above it in the upper tail; standardized residuals beyond 3: `r n_big_resid` | No meaningful departure from normality |
| Scale-location | Nearly flat; residual standard deviation (SD) is `r resid_sd[["Adelie"]]` g for Adelies, `r resid_sd[["Chinstrap"]]` g for Chinstraps, `r resid_sd[["Gentoo"]]` g for Gentoos | Modest heteroscedasticity by species; robust standard errors would be a reasonable sensitivity check |
| Residuals vs leverage | Largest Cook's distance `r signif(cooks_max, 2)`, far below the conventional 0.5 | No single bird drives the fit |

: What the standard diagnostics show for the penguin model.
{#tbl-penguins-diagnostics}

The plots are not featureless, and the features are small. The
discipline is the same on clinical data, where they are rarely
small: check, name each pattern, and decide whether it changes the
conclusion.

### What the four plots cannot show

The standard plots look only at the variables in the model. A
variable left out shows up only when you plot the residuals
against it, and `sex` is the obvious candidate:

```{r}
#| label: fig-penguins-resid-sex
#| fig-cap: "Residuals of the main-effects model by sex, within
#|   species. The model omits sex, and its residuals separate by
#|   it, strongly in Adelies and Gentoos and weakly in Chinstraps."
#| fig-alt: "Strip plot of model residuals, one panel per species,
#|   with female and male penguins side by side. In the Adelie and
#|   Gentoo panels the female residuals sit mostly below zero and
#|   the male residuals mostly above, with little overlap; in the
#|   Chinstrap panel the two groups overlap heavily."
#| fig-scap: "Residuals by sex, within species"
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.5
penguins_resid <- penguins_clean |>
  dplyr::mutate(resid = residuals(fit)) |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(sex))

ggplot(penguins_resid, aes(sex, resid, color = sex)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey60") +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Dark2", guide = "none") +
  facet_wrap(~ species) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Residual (g)")
```

```{r}
#| label: penguins-resid-sex-gap
#| echo: false
sex_gap <- round(diff(tapply(penguins_resid$resid,
                             penguins_resid$sex, mean)), -1)
```

Males sit on average `r sex_gap` g above females at the same
flipper length and species. The gap is large in Adelies and
Gentoos and small in Chinstraps, which is itself a finding a
report should mention. The four standard plots gave no
hint
of it, because the residuals' overall distribution is a symmetric
mixture of two shifted groups and passes for normal. Whether to
add `sex` depends on the question. To describe mass as a function
of flipper length within species, the model stands, and the sex
structure belongs in the report. To predict mass, add `sex` and
handle its missing values as the LLM prompt above lays out.

::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'}
**Four clean diagnostic plots do not mean a well-specified
model.** They test the shape of the residuals against the fitted
values, not whether a variable is missing. An omitted variable
whose effect is roughly symmetric hides inside residuals that look
normal and evenly spread. Plot the residuals against every
candidate variable you left out.
:::

### The interaction model

```{r}
#| label: penguins-aic-drop
#| echo: false
aic_drop <- AIC(fit) -
  AIC(lm(body_mass_g ~ flipper_length_mm * species,
         data = penguins_clean))
```

Resist over-modeling. The main-effects model fits well; an
interaction model, `body_mass_g ~ flipper_length_mm * species`,
gives each species its own slope at the cost of two parameters.
Its AIC (Akaike information criterion) is `r round(aic_drop, 1)`
lower. An AIC difference of $\Delta$ gives the simpler model a
relative likelihood of $e^{-\Delta/2}$ against the larger one, here
about `r signif(exp(-aic_drop / 2), 2)`, which favors the larger
model without settling the matter. Whether to report it depends on
whether different slopes make biological sense (different body
shapes make them plausible), on whether the goal is description or
prediction, and on the audience. The defensible choice is to
report both, with the AIC comparison, and let the reader see the
trade-off; reporting the larger model because it has more p-values
is the wrong reason.

### What the model licenses you to say

The coefficient of `r flipper_slope` g per mm is an association.
It is tempting to call it 'the effect of flipper length on body
mass', and the word 'effect' claims something the analysis cannot
support. @fig-penguins-dag sketches the plausible causal structure:
species and sex each influence both flipper length and body mass,
and both measurements grow with the bird's overall size, which is
not measured.

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%| label: fig-penguins-dag
%%| fig-alt: "Directed acyclic graph with five nodes. Species, sex,
%%|   and overall body size each have arrows into both flipper length
%%|   and body mass. Overall body size is marked unmeasured. There is
%%|   no arrow from flipper length to body mass."
%%| fig-cap: "A plausible causal graph for the penguin measurements.
%%|   Flipper length and body mass share causes, one of them
%%|   unmeasured; no arrow runs from one to the other."
flowchart TD
  SP["Species"] --> FL["Flipper length"]
  SP --> BM["Body mass"]
  SX["Sex"] --> FL
  SX --> BM
  SZ["Overall size<br/><i>unmeasured</i>"] --> FL
  SZ --> BM
```

A causal question needs a hypothetical experiment that would
answer it, the **target trial** [@hernan2016target]: who would be
enrolled, what would be assigned, and what would be measured. No
such trial exists for 'assign a penguin a longer flipper', so the
question is descriptive, and the honest verbs are 'is associated
with' and 'predicts'. The opposite error matters as much. When a
study's goal *is* causal, as in an observational comparison of two
treatments, calling the estimate an association does not make the
analysis less causal; it only hides the assumptions the reader
needs to judge it. Hernán's argument against that euphemism
[@hernan2018cword] is short and worth reading before your first
observational analysis. Habit 11 (@sec-habits) states the rule:
match the verb to the design.

### Exercises

2. Extend the analysis: fit the interaction model
   `body_mass_g ~ flipper_length_mm * species`. Test the
   interaction, and report the AIC against the main-effects model.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
```{r}
#| label: soln-23-1
#| message: false
main <- lm(body_mass_g ~ flipper_length_mm + species,
           data = penguins_clean)
inter <- lm(body_mass_g ~ flipper_length_mm * species,
            data = penguins_clean)

anova(main, inter)
AIC(main, inter)
```

The interaction asks whether the mass-per-millimeter slope differs
by species, not whether the species differ in mass. The `anova()`
F-test and the AIC comparison answer the same question two ways,
and they should agree; where they disagree, the difference is
small enough that the choice is not doing any work. Report the
comparison you pre-specified, not the one that came out better.
:::

3. Fit a multinomial regression of `species` on the four
   morphometric measurements, and report how often it recovers the
   observed species.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
```{r}
#| label: soln-23-3
#| message: false
#| results: hide
fit_mn <- nnet::multinom(
  species ~ bill_length_mm + bill_depth_mm +
            flipper_length_mm + body_mass_g,
  data = penguins_clean)
```

```{r}
#| label: soln-23-3-out
predicted <- predict(fit_mn)
tab <- table(observed = penguins_clean$species, predicted)
tab
round(sum(diag(tab)) / sum(tab), 3)
```

Every penguin is classified correctly, which the scatter plot
already implied: the three species separate cleanly in
morphometric space.

An accuracy of exactly 1 should make you suspicious rather than
pleased. The number is resubstitution on the data the model was
fitted to, with four continuous predictors and well-separated
groups, so it measures how flexible the model is at least as much
as how learnable the species are. Report it as what the exercise
asked for, how often the model recovers the observed species, and
never as predictive accuracy. That claim needs cross-validation or
a held-out set, and would come back lower.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** The `speciesGentoo` coefficient is `r gentoo_coef` g.
A draft results paragraph says 'Gentoo penguins were
`r gentoo_coef` g heavier than Adelies'. What is wrong, and how do
you fix the sentence?

**Answer.** The coefficient is the difference *at equal flipper
length*; the raw difference in mean mass is about
`r format(gentoo_gap, big.mark = ",")` g. Either report the raw
difference as a description, or say 'at the same flipper length,
Gentoos were `r gentoo_coef` g heavier on average than Adelies'.
The draft's sentence also says 'were heavier', which is a
description of these birds; it should not become 'species
increases mass'.
:::

## Test, report, and automate {#sec-penguins-test}

### Tests on the data and the model

The checks so far ran once, in this chapter. A compendium needs
them to run every time the analysis does, so they belong in a test
file. Following Habit 9, the tests below check statistics, not
shapes: the denominator, the factor levels the model's reference
category depends on, and the slope itself, re-derived by an
independent route. The within-species slope of a model with a
common slope equals the pooled within-species covariance of flipper
length and mass divided by the pooled within-species variance of
flipper length, so it can be computed without `lm()`.

```{r}
#| label: penguins-tests
#| eval: false
# inst/tinytest/test-penguins-model.R
penguins_clean <- tidyr::drop_na(palmerpenguins::penguins,
                                 body_mass_g, flipper_length_mm)
fit <- lm(body_mass_g ~ flipper_length_mm + species,
          data = penguins_clean)

expect_equal(nrow(penguins_clean), 342L,
             info = "only the two rows missing a modeled variable dropped")
expect_equal(sum(is.na(penguins_clean$sex)), 9L,
             info = "rows missing only sex are kept")
expect_identical(levels(penguins_clean$species),
                 c("Adelie", "Chinstrap", "Gentoo"),
                 info = "Adelie is the reference level")
expect_equal(nobs(fit), nrow(penguins_clean),
             info = "lm() used every analytic row")

by_species <- split(penguins_clean, penguins_clean$species)
sxy <- sum(vapply(by_species, \(d) {
  sum((d$flipper_length_mm - mean(d$flipper_length_mm)) *
        (d$body_mass_g - mean(d$body_mass_g)))
}, numeric(1)))
sxx <- sum(vapply(by_species, \(d) {
  sum((d$flipper_length_mm - mean(d$flipper_length_mm))^2)
}, numeric(1)))
expect_equal(unname(coef(fit)["flipper_length_mm"]), sxy / sxx,
             info = "slope equals the pooled within-species estimate")

ci <- confint(fit)["flipper_length_mm", ]
expect_true(ci[1] > 0,
            info = "the within-species association is positive")
```

The expected counts (342 and 9) are written into the test on
purpose. They are the denominator the methods section states, and
the test exists to fail if a later change to the cleaning moves
it. In a project the chunk is the file
`inst/tinytest/test-penguins-model.R`; the chunk below writes it
to a temporary file and runs it as `tinytest` would.

```{r}
#| label: penguins-tests-run
library(tinytest)

test_file <- file.path(tempdir(), "test-penguins-model.R")
writeLines(knitr::knit_code$get("penguins-tests"), test_file)
run_test_file(test_file, verbose = 0)
```

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
A test suite that has never failed has not been shown to work.
Plant the bug from the cleaning Pitfall, dropping every incomplete
row, and confirm that the suite catches it.

```{r}
#| label: penguins-tests-mutant
mutant_file <- file.path(tempdir(), "test-penguins-mutant.R")
mutant <- sub("tidyr::drop_na(palmerpenguins::penguins,",
              "tidyr::drop_na(palmerpenguins::penguins)",
              knitr::knit_code$get("penguins-tests"), fixed = TRUE)
mutant <- sub("^ +body_mass_g, flipper_length_mm\\)$", "", mutant)
writeLines(mutant, mutant_file)
mutant_results <- run_test_file(mutant_file, verbose = 0)
stopifnot(any(!as.logical(mutant_results)))
mutant_results
```

The denominator and the kept-`sex` tests fail; the slope test
passes, because the slope is recomputed from the same, wrong,
data. That is why the suite needs both kinds of test.
:::

### The paper

The compendium's manuscript, `analysis/paper/paper.qmd`, is short
and contains no new analysis. Its setup chunk loads the data,
applies the same `drop_na()`, and fits the same model; its Methods
section states the denominator with inline code
(`{{r}} nrow(penguins_clean)`, and the number dropped as a
difference), and its Results section cross-references the scatter
plot and a coefficient table produced by `broom::tidy()`. The full
pattern, a Quarto document whose every number is computed, is the
worked example of @sec-quarto-worked; the compendium layout that
holds it is in @sec-zzcollab-assemble. Rendering inside the
container (display-only) reproduces the paper from raw data to
typeset output:

```bash
make docker-render REPORT=analysis/paper/paper.qmd
```

::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'}
Ask for a draft results paragraph, and treat it as a draft.

> **Context.** Below are the output of
> `broom::tidy(fit, conf.int = TRUE)` and `broom::glance(fit)` for
> `lm(body_mass_g ~ flipper_length_mm + species)` fitted to
> `palmerpenguins` (Adelie is the reference level), and the
> species means of body mass and flipper length.
>
> **Constraints.** Report estimates with 95% confidence intervals,
> not p-values alone. Use 'is associated with', never 'effect' or
> 'increases'. Write every number as a Quarto inline expression
> (`{{r}} ...`) referring to `fit`, not as a literal.
>
> **Criteria.** State that species coefficients are differences at
> equal flipper length, and give the raw species difference beside
> the adjusted one. Name Adelie as the reference.

*Failure mode.* Models report the adjusted species coefficient as
the species difference, call the slope an effect, or type numbers
that are rounded differently from the table. *Check.* Render the
paragraph, change the data (drop the Gentoo rows) and render
again: every number must change. Then read the paragraph against
the Check at the end of @sec-penguins-model.
:::

### Continuous integration

CI (continuous integration) runs the tests and the render on every
push, so that a change that moves the denominator turns a check red
before anyone reads the paper. The workflow is the one in
@sec-testing-ci with a render step added (display-only;
@sec-ci covers the rest):

```yaml
# .github/workflows/check.yaml
name: check
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r@v2
      - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-renv@v2
      - uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/setup@v2
      - name: Run tests
        run: |
          Rscript -e 'res <- tinytest::run_test_dir("inst/tinytest")' \
            -e 'quit(status = as.integer(tinytest::any_fail(res)))'
      - name: Render paper
        run: quarto render analysis/paper/paper.qmd
```

`setup-renv` restores the packages in `renv.lock`, so CI runs the
versions the paper was written with. The `quit()` line is what
turns a failing test into a failing job (@sec-testing-ci).

### Exercises

4. Add the multinomial model of exercise 3 to the compendium as a
   second analysis script with its own test file, and confirm that
   the CI job passes, then fails when you plant a bug.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
A correct result has three parts. The script
(`analysis/scripts/02-multinom.R`) fits the model and saves the
confusion table. The test file asserts a statistic, not a shape:
for example, that the confusion table's total equals
`nrow(penguins_clean)` and that its diagonal proportion equals the
value computed by `mean(predict(fit_mn) == penguins_clean$species)`
in the test itself. The CI log shows the test file's results line,
and a commit that changes the formula (dropping
`bill_length_mm`, say) makes the job red. If the job stays green
after the planted change, the test checks something the change
does not affect.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** In the planted-bug Verification, the slope test
still passed. Why is that not a weakness of the slope test?

**Answer.** The slope test checks that `lm()` computed what it
claims from the data it was given; it re-derives the estimate
independently, which catches a wrong formula or a wrong model.
It cannot catch wrong data, because both routes see the same rows.
The denominator test catches wrong data. Each test covers a
failure the other cannot, which is why a suite needs both.
:::

## Deposit {#sec-penguins-deposit}

A tag marks the commit the paper was rendered from; an archive
gives it a DOI (digital object identifier) that outlives the
repository (@sec-federal). From the shell (display-only):

```bash
git tag -a v1.0 -m "Penguins case study, complete"
git push origin v1.0
```

With the Zenodo integration enabled for the repository (configured
once in the Zenodo account settings), publishing a GitHub release
from the tag archives the repository at that commit and mints a
DOI. The deposit is the repository at the tagged commit; its
README answers four questions:

| README section | Content |
|---|---|
| What | One paragraph on the question and the dataset |
| How to reproduce | `make docker-build`, then `make docker-render REPORT=analysis/paper/paper.qmd` |
| Where the data are | In the `palmerpenguins` package, at the version in `renv.lock` |
| How to cite | The DOI and the authors |

: The four questions a deposit README answers.
{#tbl-penguins-readme}

A reader given the DOI can rebuild the paper in two commands.

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
Resolve the DOI in a browser and confirm that it lands on the
archived release, not the live repository, and that the archived
files include `renv.lock` and the Dockerfile. Then clone the
tagged commit into a new directory and run the two README
commands; the rendered numbers should match the paper's.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** Why archive on Zenodo when the repository is already
public on GitHub?

**Answer.** Hosting is not archiving. A GitHub repository can be
renamed, rewritten, or deleted, and its URL then points nowhere; a
Zenodo record is preserved under a DOI that cites one fixed
version, which is what a paper's citation needs.
:::

## Rules of thumb

1. **Habit 1: the compendium is the unit.** Scaffold before the
   first line of analysis code, and deposit the whole compendium,
   not the paper.
2. **Habit 9: test the statistics, not the shape.** Assert the
   denominator and re-derive a key estimate; a column-exists test
   passes on a wrong answer.
3. **Habit 11: match the verb to the design.** A cross-sectional
   coefficient is an association; say so, and say why.

## Cumulative practice

5. *Cumulative (uses @sec-docker).* Reproduce this chapter's
   compendium from scratch: scaffold it, add the cleaning, model,
   paper, tests, and CI workflow, and render it inside the
   container. Confirm that every number in the rendered paper
   matches the numbers in this chapter, and that the test suite
   catches the planted bug from @sec-penguins-test.
6. *On your own work (no key).* Deposit a compendium of your own to
   Zenodo, and confirm that the DOI resolves to the archived
   release and that the README is the first thing a reader sees.

## Cheat sheet

| Step | Command | Check |
|---|---|---|
| Scaffold | `zzc tidyverse`, or the layout of @sec-zzcollab-assemble | Pillar audit passes |
| Map missingness | `naniar::vis_miss(df)` | Pattern explained |
| Drop for the model | `tidyr::drop_na(df, y, x)` | `nrow()` matches the methods |
| Table 1 | `gtsummary::tbl_summary(df, by = group)` | Missing shown as a row |
| Fit | `lm(y ~ x + group, data = df)` | Reference level stated |
| Diagnose | `plot(fit)`; residuals against omitted variables | Each pattern named |
| Test | `tinytest::run_test_dir("inst/tinytest")` | A planted bug fails |
| Render | `make docker-render REPORT=analysis/paper/paper.qmd` | Numbers change when data change |
| Tag | `git tag -a v1.0 -m "..."` | `git show v1.0` |
| Deposit | GitHub release with Zenodo enabled | DOI resolves |

: The analysis arc at a glance. {#tbl-penguins-cheat-sheet}

## Prerequisites answers {#sec-quiz-answers-23}

1. `palmerpenguins::penguins` contains
   `r sum(!complete.cases(penguins))` rows with at least one
   missing value (most commonly `sex`). First document the
   missing pattern (`naniar::vis_miss()`), then choose a strategy
   before analysis. Drop only rows missing a variable the model
   uses. Complete case is then defensible when missingness
   plausibly does not depend on the outcome given the covariates,
   as the chapter argues it does not here; that, not MCAR
   (missing completely at random) or a percentage threshold, is
   the condition. Multiple imputation is
   preferable when missingness may depend on the outcome or when
   the dropped rows carry precision worth recovering.
2. A research compendium (@sec-zzcollab): the Five Pillars,
   assembled by hand from the `rrtools` layout, `renv`, and the
   canonical Dockerfile, or automated, for example with
   `mkdir penguins && cd penguins && zzc tidyverse`. The analysis
   code goes in `analysis/scripts/`, the manuscript in
   `analysis/paper/`, and the tests in `inst/tinytest/`.
3. A residuals-vs-fitted plot. It reveals non-linearity,
   non-constant variance, and systematic lack of fit in a single
   view. Read it, and the other three diagnostic plots, for what
   they actually show, then plot the residuals against variables
   the model omits; only then interpret the regression coefficient
   as the association between flipper length and body mass.
